We compute the Z -> gamma gamma partial widthin the framework of the recently proposed renormalizable gauge sector of the noncommutative standard model. The one-loop renormalizability is obtained for the model containing the usual six representations of matter fields of the first generation. Even more, the noncommutative part is finite or free of divergences, showing that perhaps new interaction symmetry exists in the noncommutative gauge sector of the model. The proposed decay process \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\) is forbidden in the Standard Model. This is because a neutral spin-1 gauge boson cannot decay into two identical massless photons within the ordinary commutative framework. As a result, any observation of such a decay would be a clear indication of physics beyond the Standard Model. In particular, it could provide evidence for noncommutative space-time coordinates at very short distances, where the usual notion of continuous space-time may break down.

Within the framework of the noncommutative Standard Model, the partial decay width for \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\) can be computed using the renormalizable gauge sector of the theory. Noncommutative extensions of gauge theories modify the interactions among gauge bosons and can generate new vertices that are absent in the ordinary Standard Model. One such interaction is a direct coupling between the \(Z\) boson and two photons, allowing the otherwise forbidden decay \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\) to occur.

A consistent treatment of this process requires the underlying theory to be renormalizable. At the one-loop level, renormalizability is achieved in a model that contains the usual six matter-field representations of the first generation. These representations correspond to the standard fermionic content of one generation of the Standard Model and ensure that the quantum corrections remain under control. This makes it possible to perform meaningful calculations of rare processes such as \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\) within the noncommutative framework.

An important feature of the noncommutative contribution to the \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\) decay width is that it is finite, or divergence-free. This absence of divergences suggests that the noncommutative gauge sector may possess a deeper organizing principle. In particular, it may point toward the existence of a new interaction symmetry that controls the structure of the theory and protects certain observables from ultraviolet divergences.

Experimental searches for the decay \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\) can therefore be used to constrain the scale at which noncommutative effects become relevant. Since no such decay has been observed, current experimental analyses place a firm lower bound on the noncommutativity scale. This bound is approximately \(1\ \text{TeV}\), indicating that if space-time noncommutativity exists, it must become significant only at energies at or above the tera-electron-volt scale.

The decay of the \(Z\) boson into two photons, \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\), is strictly forbidden in the ordinary Standard Model. This follows from the structure of the Standard Model gauge interactions and, in particular, from the absence of a neutral triple-gauge-boson coupling of the form \(Z\gamma\gamma\). For this reason, any observation of such a process would represent a clear signal of physics beyond the Standard Model.

The text proposes using this forbidden decay as a sensitive probe of possible short-distance noncommutativity of space-time coordinates. In noncommutative field theories, the space-time coordinates no longer commute, but instead satisfy a relation of the form
\[
[x^\mu,x^\nu] = i\theta^{\mu\nu},
\]
where \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\) is a constant antisymmetric tensor that characterizes the scale and direction of noncommutativity. Such a modification can generate new interactions that are absent in the conventional Standard Model, including neutral gauge-boson vertices. As a result, the decay \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\), although forbidden in the Standard Model, may become possible in a noncommutative extension of it.

The analysis is carried out within a recently proposed renormalizable noncommutative version of the Standard Model gauge sector. This framework allows one to compute corrections arising from noncommutative geometry in a controlled way. In particular, the authors calculate the contribution of noncommutative interactions to the partial decay width of the process \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\). The calculation shows that the noncommutative contribution is finite, meaning that no additional divergences appear in this decay amplitude at the order considered. This finiteness is significant because it suggests that the structure of the noncommutative gauge sector may contain a previously unnoticed symmetry or organizing principle governing these new interactions.

The resulting decay width depends on the scale of noncommutativity, usually denoted by \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{NC}}\). This scale determines the energy at which noncommutative effects become important. If \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{NC}}\) is very large, the new effects are strongly suppressed and the decay rate becomes too small to observe. Conversely, if the scale is near the electroweak or TeV range, the decay could potentially produce measurable deviations from Standard Model expectations.

By comparing the theoretical prediction for the \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\) decay rate with available experimental limits, the text derives a lower bound on the noncommutativity scale. The analysis indicates that current data require
\[
\Lambda_{\mathrm{NC}} \gtrsim 1~\text{TeV}.
\]
This means that if noncommutative space-time effects exist, they must be suppressed at least up to energies of approximately one tera-electronvolt.

Overall, the study presents \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\) as a clean and theoretically well-motivated channel for testing noncommutative extensions of the Standard Model. Since the decay is forbidden in the ordinary theory, even a small observed signal would be highly significant. The finiteness of the calculated noncommutative contribution also points toward a possible new interaction symmetry in the renormalizable noncommutative gauge sector, making this process relevant not only phenomenologically but also for understanding the theoretical structure of noncommutative field theories.

**The Even Discovery**

The world often changes through small moments of curiosity. A question, a mistake, or a quiet observation can lead to something unexpected. This is the heart of discovery: finding meaning where others may see nothing unusual.

Even the simplest experiences can open the door to new ideas. A walk through nature can reveal patterns in leaves, clouds, or stars. A conversation can inspire a new way of thinking. The greatest discoveries do not always begin in laboratories or books; sometimes they begin with wonder.

The discovery of something new reminds us that learning never ends. Every answer can lead to another question, and every question can guide us toward deeper understanding. Even when the path is uncertain, curiosity helps us move forward.

In this way, discovery is not only about finding new places or facts. It is also about seeing the world with fresh eyes and recognizing that even ordinary moments can become extraordinary.

**Abstract**

We investigate the forbidden decay \(Z	o\gamma\gamma\) as a sensitive probe of spacetime noncommutativity in the noncommutative Standard Model. While this channel is excluded in ordinary Lorentz-invariant quantum field theory by the Landau–Yang theorem, the presence of a constant noncommutativity tensor \(	heta^{\mu
u}\) violates Lorentz invariance and induces novel neutral triple-gauge-boson interactions at leading order in the noncommutative scale \(\Lambda_{m NC}^{-2}\). We compute the corresponding \(Z\gamma\gamma\) vertex in a renormalizable formulation of the noncommutative Standard Model and show that the noncommutative contribution to the decay amplitude is finite, requiring no additional counterterms in the neutral gauge sector at the order considered. The resulting decay width depends on the orientation and magnitude of \(	heta^{\mu
u}\), leading to characteristic Lorentz-violating angular and possible sidereal-time signatures. Using present experimental limits on rare \(Z\)-boson decays, we derive a lower bound on the noncommutativity scale of order \(\Lambda_{m NC}\sim 1\ {m TeV}\), with the precise value depending on the gauge-sector parameters and the assumed structure of \(	heta^{\mu

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a research article about the decay \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\) in the renormalizable gauge sector of the noncommutative Standard Model, emphasizing why it is forbidden in the Standard Model and how it constrains the noncommutativity scale.
counterfactuals.output:
The article studies the rare decay

\[
Z \to \gamma\gamma
\]

in the gauge sector of the noncommutative Standard Model, where space-time coordinates satisfy

\[
[x^\mu,x^\nu]= i\,\theta^{\mu\nu}\sim \frac{i}{\Lambda_{\rm NC}^2}.
\]

Here \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\) is a fixed antisymmetric tensor and \(\Lambda_{\rm NC}\) is the energy scale at which noncommutative effects become important.

## Why \(Z\to\gamma\gamma\) is forbidden in the ordinary Standard Model

In the usual Lorentz-invariant Standard Model, the decay of an on-shell spin-1 particle into two identical on-shell photons is forbidden by the Landau–Yang theorem. The theorem relies on:

- Lorentz invariance,
- Bose symmetry of the two photons,
- electromagnetic gauge invariance,
- the photons being identical massless spin-1 particles.

As a result, an on-shell \(Z\) boson cannot decay into two real photons in the Standard Model. There is also no tree-level neutral triple gauge-boson coupling of the form \(Z\gamma\gamma\), and loop contributions vanish consistently with the Landau–Yang theorem.

Thus,

\[
\Gamma_{\rm SM}(Z\to\gamma\gamma)=0.
\]

Observation of this decay would therefore be a clean signal of physics beyond the Standard Model.

## How noncommutativity allows the decay

In the noncommutative Standard Model, ordinary products of fields are replaced by Moyal star products. This modifies gauge interactions and can generate neutral triple gauge-boson vertices that are absent in the ordinary Standard Model, including a possible

\[
Z\gamma\gamma
\]

coupling.

The fixed tensor \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\) introduces preferred directions in space-time and therefore violates ordinary Lorentz invariance. Because Lorentz invariance is one of the assumptions behind the Landau–Yang theorem, the theorem no longer applies in the same way. Consequently, the decay

\[
Z\to\gamma\gamma
\]

can occur in the noncommutative theory.

In the renormalizable gauge sector, the strength of the \(Z\gamma\gamma\) interaction is typically parametrized by a dimensionless coefficient, often denoted schematically as \(K_{Z\gamma\gamma}\). The decay width has the characteristic scaling

\[
\Gamma(Z\to\gamma\gamma)
\propto
\alpha\, M_Z
\left(\frac{M_Z}{\Lambda_{\rm NC}}\right)^4
K_{Z\gamma\gamma}^2 ,
\]

or, more explicitly in common normalizations,

\[
\Gamma(Z\to\gamma\gamma)
\simeq
\frac{\alpha}{4}
\frac{M_Z^5}{\Lambda_{\rm NC}^4}
\sin^2(2\theta_W)
K_{Z\gamma\gamma}^2 .
\]

The important point is the strong suppression by

\[
\Lambda_{\rm NC}^{-4}.
\]

So even a relatively small experimental upper limit on the branching ratio can place a meaningful lower bound on the noncommutativity scale.

## Constraint on the noncommutativity scale

Experimentally, no \(Z\to\gamma\gamma\) signal has been observed. LEP bounds give an upper limit on the branching ratio at roughly the level

\[
{\rm Br}(Z\to\gamma\gamma) \lesssim 10^{-5}.
\]

Using

\[
{\rm Br}(Z\to\gamma\gamma)
=
\frac{\Gamma(Z\to\gamma\gamma)}{\Gamma_Z},
\]

one obtains a lower bound of the form

\[
\Lambda_{\rm NC}
\gtrsim
\left[
\frac{\alpha M_Z^5 \sin^2(2\theta_W)}
{4\,\Gamma_Z\,{\rm Br}_{\rm exp}}
K_{Z\gamma\gamma}^2
\right]^{1/4}.
\]

Numerically, for a coupling \(K_{Z\gamma\gamma}\) of order unity, the present bound is typically in the few-hundred-GeV to TeV range, depending on the precise normalization and allowed parameter region of the renormalizable noncommutative gauge sector.

The scaling is especially important:

\[
\Lambda_{\rm NC}\propto
{\rm Br}(Z\to\gamma\gamma)^{-1/4}.
\]

Therefore, even large improvements in the branching-ratio sensitivity translate into more modest, but still significant, improvements in the bound on \(\Lambda_{\rm NC}\). Future high-statistics \(Z\)-factories could push the sensitivity to much smaller branching ratios and probe noncommutativity scales in the multi-TeV range.

## Main conclusion

The article emphasizes that \(Z\to\gamma\gamma\) is a null process in the ordinary Standard Model because of the Landau–Yang theorem, but it becomes allowed in the noncommutative Standard Model because the background tensor \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\) breaks ordinary Lorentz invariance and induces neutral triple gauge-boson couplings. The non-observation of the decay therefore provides a clean constraint on the scale of space-time noncommutativity, \(\Lambda_{\rm NC}\), with the decay rate suppressed as \(\Lambda_{\rm NC}^{-4}\).
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
We study the rare decay \(Z\to\gamma\gamma\) as a null-test probe of spacetime noncommutativity at short distances, where coordinate operators obey
\[
[x^\mu,x^\nu]= i\theta^{\mu\nu}.
\]
In ordinary Lorentz-invariant quantum field theory this channel is forbidden by the Landau–Yang theorem and is absent in the Standard Model, making any observation a clean signal of new spacetime structure. In noncommutative gauge theories, however, the \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\)-dependent deformation of gauge interactions induces neutral triple-gauge-boson couplings such as \(Z\gamma\gamma\), allowing \(Z\to\gamma\gamma\) at leading order in the noncommutativity scale \(\Lambda_{\rm NC}\sim |\theta|^{-1/2}\).

We discuss the structure of the effective \(Z\gamma\gamma\) vertex in \(\theta\)-expanded noncommutative Standard Model frameworks and emphasize the role of gauge invariance, Lorentz-violating tensor contractions, and angular anisotropies as characteristic observables. Theoretical consistency is addressed through one-loop renormalizability: while generic noncommutative extensions suffer from UV/IR mixing and operator proliferation, specific \(\theta\)-expanded gauge-sector constructions can be renormalizable at one loop for constrained choices of representations and trace prescriptions, with counterterms preserving the deformed gauge symmetry.

Current experimental non-observation of \(Z\to\gamma\gamma\), together with precision electroweak and collider bounds on anomalous neutral gauge couplings, places lower limits on \(\Lambda_{\rm NC}\), typically in the multi-TeV range depending on the embedding and orientation of \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\). Future high-luminosity \(Z\)-factories and precision measurements of forbidden neutral decays could therefore provide sensitive probes of noncommutative geometry beyond direct energy reach.

counterfactuals.prompt: In the style of a particle physics journal abstract, describe a study computing the partial width of \(Z \to \gamma\gamma\) in a recently proposed renormalizable noncommutative Standard Model gauge sector with first-generation matter representations.
counterfactuals.output:
We present a calculation of the rare decay \(Z\to\gamma\gamma\) in the gauge sector of a recently proposed renormalizable noncommutative extension of the Standard Model, with matter fields assigned to first-generation representations. In contrast to the ordinary Standard Model, where the decay is forbidden for an on-shell \(Z\) boson into two identical photons, the noncommutative deformation induces neutral triple-gauge-boson interactions through the Seiberg--Witten map and the constant antisymmetric tensor \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\). The resulting \(Z\gamma\gamma\) vertex is evaluated at leading order in the noncommutativity parameter, \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\sim \Lambda_{\rm NC}^{-2}\).

Using the renormalizable gauge-action parameters fixed by the chosen matter representation content, we derive the on-shell decay amplitude, verify electromagnetic Ward identities, and compute the corresponding two-body phase-space integral. The partial width is found to scale as  
\[
\Gamma(Z\to\gamma\gamma)\;\propto\;
\alpha\, m_Z^5\,\Lambda_{\rm NC}^{-4}\,
\left|K_{Z\gamma\gamma}\right|^2 ,
\]
where \(K_{Z\gamma\gamma}\) denotes the model-dependent neutral triple-gauge coupling determined by the noncommutative Standard Model embedding. The result depends on the Lorentz-violating background components of \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\), and vanishes smoothly in the commutative limit \(\Lambda_{\rm NC}\to\infty\).

We discuss the phenomenological implications of the predicted width for current bounds on exotic \(Z\)-boson decays. Although the branching ratio is strongly suppressed for noncommutativity scales in the TeV range, the channel provides a clean probe of noncommutative neutral gauge interactions and of the representation-dependent structure required by renormalizability.
